    E01 — A secondary substation and its low-voltage network¶

    This case study computes the earthing of a 10/0.4 kV secondary substation (German Ortsnetzstation) together with the TN low-voltage network it feeds: 30 single-family houses whose foundation earth electrodes are bonded to the station earth through the PEN conductors, in two-layer soil. It is written for grounding engineers who want numbers, and it answers five questions:

    1. How much does the low-voltage network lower the earthing impedance at the station (the global earthing effect), and how does that depend on the number of houses and on the soil?
    2. What earth potential rise and which touch voltages does an earth fault on the medium-voltage side of the station cause, with and without the network?
    3. Which potentials does the PEN transfer to the houses, and where in the network is the touch voltage largest?
    4. What changes at 1 kHz?
    5. How far can the numbers be trusted?

    The building blocks are explained in the tutorials and are not repeated here: T03 (input, cluster and electrode impedance, split factor), T06 (the network generator), T04 (frequency response) and T08 (touch voltages and EN 50522). The network is one point of the parameter space of the AP1 studies (see the glossary) for which the generators were built: a station, house connections and cable cabinets in two-layer soil.

    Runtime: about 70 s.

    In [1]:
    Copied!

import groundfield as gf
from groundfield.generators import (
    HomogeneousSoilSpec,

    TnNetworkGenerator,
    TwoLayerSoilSpec,

print("groundfield", gf.__version__)

    The model¶

    Part Model Generator setting
    station earth ring of 4 m radius, 0.6 m deep; four 2.5 m rods on a 2 m circle; bonded SubstationConfig default
    houses 30 foundation earth electrodes, 10 m × 10 m, 2 × 2 meshes, 0.8 m deep, bare residential default
    layout three rows of ten houses, 25 m apart, rows 30 m apart; the station in the centre ManhattanGridPlacement default
    cable cabinets two, at the far ends of the two halves, one 1.5 m rod each CabinetConfig default
    PEN copper, 78.5 mm², insulated, 0.6 m deep, inductive PenConfig(inductance_model="neumann")
    soil \(\rho_1\) = 200 Ω·m, \(h_1\) = 5 m, over \(\rho_2\) = 30 Ω·m TwoLayerSoilSpec

    Station. The HV protective earth and the LV system earth of the station form one common earthing system, as usual in TN networks. The LV neutral, and with it the PEN of every outgoing cable, is bonded to the station earth.

    Network. Each of the two cable cabinets (German KVS) has a PEN main of its own from the station (star topology). The mains run along the centre row and are joined to its houses; the houses of the outer rows are connected to the main of their half by service drops. The foundations are modelled bare; the effect of their concrete encasement is the topic of case study E02.

    PEN. A wire of 5 mm radius, insulated from the soil (no leakage), cut into 5 m pieces. The pieces carry their self and mutual inductances (Neumann's formula) and the earth-return correction of the conducting soil (sommerfeld, the default). The inductance makes the network frequency dependent.

    Soil. A resistive top layer (dry sand) over a conductive bottom (water-bearing ground). It is one of the soils of the AP1 study grid, in which \(\rho_1\) runs from 30 to 1000 Ω·m, \(\rho_2\) from 30 to 200 Ω·m and \(h_1\) from 5 to 30 m; section 1 varies it.

    Fault. An earth fault on the MV side of the station drives a current \(I_E\) into the station earth, which returns through remote earth to the infeeding substation. The model feeds 1 A into the station cluster. The field problem is linear, so every voltage is first given per ampere of \(I_E\) (in V/A, numerically an impedance) and scaled in section 2.

    Engines. Two-layer soil and wire electrodes call for the default image engine, which forwards to image_2layer: closed-form kernels, cheap, and accurate for impedances. Its current model, one uniform current per straight wire, is not accurate enough for surface potentials next to meshes and bonded clusters (T08), and both the foundations and the station are such clusters. For touch voltages the network is therefore solved a second time with mom, which carries one current per segment. Both use 1 m segments; section 5 checks that choice.

    In [2]:
    Copied! 
    SOIL = TwoLayerSoilSpec(rho_1=200.0, rho_2=30.0, h_1=5.0)


def network(n_houses=30, soil=SOIL):
    # The generator's TN network with an inductive PEN.
    config = TnNetworkConfig(
        soil=soil,
        building_counts={"residential": n_houses},
        pen=PenConfig(inductance_model="neumann"),
    )
    return TnNetworkGenerator(config, seed=1).build()


def station_alone(soil=SOIL):
    # The same station earth without any connection to the LV network.
    alone = gf.create_world(soil=soil.to_soil(np.random.default_rng(0)))
    grounding = TnNetworkConfig().substation.grounding
    anchor = grounding.build_at(alone, (0.0, 0.0), "trafo", np.random.default_rng(0))
    gf.create_source(alone, attached_to=anchor, magnitude=1.0)
    return alone


world = network()
STATION = world.sources[0].attached_to
HOUSES = [e.name for e in world.electrodes if e.name.endswith("_foundation_0")]
pen = [c for c in world.conductors if c.conductor_type == "pen"]
print(
    f"{len(world.electrodes)} electrode wires, {len(HOUSES)} houses, source into {STATION!r}"
)
print(f"{len(pen)} PEN sections, {sum(c.length for c in pen):.0f} m of PEN in all")
    SOIL = TwoLayerSoilSpec(rho_1=200.0, rho_2=30.0, h_1=5.0) def network(n_houses=30, soil=SOIL): # The generator's TN network with an inductive PEN. config = TnNetworkConfig( soil=soil, building_counts={"residential": n_houses}, pen=PenConfig(inductance_model="neumann"), ) return TnNetworkGenerator(config, seed=1).build() def station_alone(soil=SOIL): # The same station earth without any connection to the LV network. alone = gf.create_world(soil=soil.to_soil(np.random.default_rng(0))) grounding = TnNetworkConfig().substation.grounding anchor = grounding.build_at(alone, (0.0, 0.0), "trafo", np.random.default_rng(0)) gf.create_source(alone, attached_to=anchor, magnitude=1.0) return alone world = network() STATION = world.sources[0].attached_to HOUSES = [e.name for e in world.electrodes if e.name.endswith("_foundation_0")] pen = [c for c in world.conductors if c.conductor_type == "pen"] print( f"{len(world.electrodes)} electrode wires, {len(HOUSES)} houses, source into {STATION!r}" ) print(f"{len(pen)} PEN sections, {sum(c.length for c in pen):.0f} m of PEN in all")
    187 electrode wires, 30 houses, source into 'trafo_ring_0'
32 PEN sections, 729 m of PEN in all

    One house is added by hand: an old building at the eastern end of the network, 11.5 m beyond the eastern cable cabinet, without an earth electrode of its own. Its PEN ends on a junction at the service connection box, a node without contact to the soil. No current flows to it, so it changes nothing else in the solution; sections 2 and 3 use it.

    1 How much does the network lower the station's earthing impedance?¶

    Two numbers describe the global earthing effect:

    • the resistance \(R_\mathrm{station}\) of the station earth alone, the value a planner computes for the station without its LV connections;
    • the input impedance \(Z_\mathrm{in}\) of the network seen from the station, the impedance the fault current meets: the station, every house and both cabinets in parallel through the PEN.

    The split factor \(s\) is the share of \(I_E\) that leaves the soil through the station's own electrodes (T03).

    In [4]:
    Copied! 
    FREQUENCIES = [0.0, 50.0, 150.0, 250.0, 350.0, 550.0, 750.0, 1000.0]
F50, F1K = FREQUENCIES.index(50.0), FREQUENCIES.index(1000.0)
engine = gf.create_engine(segment_length=1.0, frequencies=FREQUENCIES)

alone = station_alone()
result = engine.solve(world)
result_alone = engine.solve(alone)

r_alone = result_alone.input_impedance()[F50].real
z_in = np.array(result.input_impedance())
s = [gf.split_factor(result, world, frequency_index=k) for k in range(len(FREQUENCIES))]
print(f"station earth alone:        R_station = {r_alone:.3f} Ohm")
print(f"station with the network:   Z_in      = {z_in[F50]:.4f} Ohm at 50 Hz")
print(f"ratio |Z_in| / R_station:   {abs(z_in[F50]) / r_alone:.2%}")
print(f"split factor of the station: |s| = {abs(s[F50]):.2%}")

share = {"station": 0.0, "houses": 0.0, "cabinets": 0.0}
for name, current in result.electrode_currents.items():
    site = "station" if name.startswith("trafo") else "houses"
    site = "cabinets" if name.startswith("kvs") else site
    share[site] += current[F50]
for site, current in share.items():
    print(f"  of 1 A, into the soil at the {site:8s}: {abs(current):.4f} A")
    FREQUENCIES = [0.0, 50.0, 150.0, 250.0, 350.0, 550.0, 750.0, 1000.0] F50, F1K = FREQUENCIES.index(50.0), FREQUENCIES.index(1000.0) engine = gf.create_engine(segment_length=1.0, frequencies=FREQUENCIES) alone = station_alone() result = engine.solve(world) result_alone = engine.solve(alone) r_alone = result_alone.input_impedance()[F50].real z_in = np.array(result.input_impedance()) s = [gf.split_factor(result, world, frequency_index=k) for k in range(len(FREQUENCIES))] print(f"station earth alone: R_station = {r_alone:.3f} Ohm") print(f"station with the network: Z_in = {z_in[F50]:.4f} Ohm at 50 Hz") print(f"ratio |Z_in| / R_station: {abs(z_in[F50]) / r_alone:.2%}") print(f"split factor of the station: |s| = {abs(s[F50]):.2%}") share = {"station": 0.0, "houses": 0.0, "cabinets": 0.0} for name, current in result.electrode_currents.items(): site = "station" if name.startswith("trafo") else "houses" site = "cabinets" if name.startswith("kvs") else site share[site] += current[F50] for site, current in share.items(): print(f" of 1 A, into the soil at the {site:8s}: {abs(current):.4f} A")

    In [5]:
    Copied! 
    # Kirchhoff: all of I_E leaves through the soil
assert abs(sum(share.values()) - 1.0) < 1e-9
assert abs(share["station"] - s[F50]) < 1e-9  # the station's share is the split factor
assert abs(z_in[F50]) < 0.05 * r_alone  # the network takes over the earthing
assert abs(share["houses"]) > 0.95
    # Kirchhoff: all of I_E leaves through the soil assert abs(sum(share.values()) - 1.0) < 1e-9 assert abs(share["station"] - s[F50]) < 1e-9 # the station's share is the split factor assert abs(z_in[F50]) < 0.05 * r_alone # the network takes over the earthing assert abs(share["houses"]) > 0.95

    The station earth alone has about 9.9 Ω. Connected to the network, the fault current meets 0.29 Ω, 2.9 % of that: the network lowers the impedance by a factor of 34. Only 1.75 % of \(I_E\) leaves the soil at the station's own electrodes, 98 % at the houses. The PEN puts the station and the 30 foundations in parallel; together they cover about 240 m × 70 m, and at that size the current reaches the conductive bottom layer (the soil comparison below shows it).

    This is the mechanism behind a global earthing system in the sense of EN 50522. Whether a real network qualifies as one is a separate assessment that this example does not make.

    How many houses does it take?¶

    The generator builds the same network with 1, 5, 10, 30 and 80 houses (the smaller ones in one row through the station, the larger ones in rows of ten); each is solved at 50 Hz and at 1 kHz.

    In [6]:
    Copied! 
    counts = [1, 5, 10, 30, 80]
sweep_engine = gf.create_engine(segment_length=1.0, frequencies=[50.0, 1000.0])
z_count = np.array([sweep_engine.solve(network(n)).input_impedance() for n in counts])
for n, (z_50, z_1k) in zip(counts, z_count, strict=True):
    print(
        f"{n:3d} houses: |Z_in| = {abs(z_50):.4f} Ohm at 50 Hz, {abs(z_1k):.4f} Ohm at 1 kHz "
        f"({abs(z_50) / r_alone:6.2%} / {abs(z_1k) / r_alone:6.2%} of the station alone)"
    )

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.8))
ax.loglog(counts, np.abs(z_count[:, 0]), "o-", label="network, 50 Hz")
ax.loglog(counts, np.abs(z_count[:, 1]), "s--", label="network, 1 kHz")
ax.axhline(r_alone, color="k", lw=0.8, ls=":", label="station alone")
ax.set_xlabel("number of houses on the PEN")
ax.set_ylabel(r"$|Z_\mathrm{in}|$ in $\Omega$")
ax.grid(True, which="both", alpha=0.3)
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
fig.tight_layout()
    counts = [1, 5, 10, 30, 80] sweep_engine = gf.create_engine(segment_length=1.0, frequencies=[50.0, 1000.0]) z_count = np.array([sweep_engine.solve(network(n)).input_impedance() for n in counts]) for n, (z_50, z_1k) in zip(counts, z_count, strict=True): print( f"{n:3d} houses: |Z_in| = {abs(z_50):.4f} Ohm at 50 Hz, {abs(z_1k):.4f} Ohm at 1 kHz " f"({abs(z_50) / r_alone:6.2%} / {abs(z_1k) / r_alone:6.2%} of the station alone)" ) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.8)) ax.loglog(counts, np.abs(z_count[:, 0]), "o-", label="network, 50 Hz") ax.loglog(counts, np.abs(z_count[:, 1]), "s--", label="network, 1 kHz") ax.axhline(r_alone, color="k", lw=0.8, ls=":", label="station alone") ax.set_xlabel("number of houses on the PEN") ax.set_ylabel(r"$|Z_\mathrm{in}|$ in $\Omega$") ax.grid(True, which="both", alpha=0.3) ax.legend(fontsize=8) fig.tight_layout()

    Copied! 
    assert np.all(np.diff(np.abs(z_count[:, 0])) < 0)  # every house lowers Z_in at 50 Hz
assert np.all(np.abs(z_count[:, 1]) > np.abs(z_count[:, 0]))  # higher at 1 kHz
assert abs(z_count[3, 0] / z_in[F50] - 1.0) < 1e-9  # 30 houses: the network above
assert abs(z_count[4, 0] / z_count[3, 0]) > 30 / 80  # slower than 1/n
    assert np.all(np.diff(np.abs(z_count[:, 0])) < 0) # every house lowers Z_in at 50 Hz assert np.all(np.abs(z_count[:, 1]) > np.abs(z_count[:, 0])) # higher at 1 kHz assert abs(z_count[3, 0] / z_in[F50] - 1.0) < 1e-9 # 30 houses: the network above assert abs(z_count[4, 0] / z_count[3, 0]) > 30 / 80 # slower than 1/n

    A single house on the PEN already lowers the impedance to 40 % of the station alone, five houses to 13 %, thirty to 2.9 %. Each further house helps less, because it stands in the potential funnels of the others: from 30 to 80 houses \(\lvert Z_\mathrm{in}\rvert\) falls to 47 % of its value, where \(1/n\) would give 38 %. At 1 kHz the curve flattens, because the reactance of the PEN limits how much the remote houses can help (section 4).

    How much does the soil matter?¶

    The same station and the same 30-house network in five soils of the AP1 grid, at 50 Hz:

    In [8]:
    Copied! 
    soils = {
    "30 over 200 Ohm m, h1 = 5 m": TwoLayerSoilSpec(rho_1=30.0, rho_2=200.0, h_1=5.0),
    "100 Ohm m, homogeneous": HomogeneousSoilSpec(rho=100.0),
    "200 over 30 Ohm m, h1 = 5 m (this case)": SOIL,
    "1000 over 30 Ohm m, h1 = 5 m": TwoLayerSoilSpec(rho_1=1000.0, rho_2=30.0, h_1=5.0),
    "1000 over 200 Ohm m, h1 = 30 m": TwoLayerSoilSpec(
        rho_1=1000.0, rho_2=200.0, h_1=30.0
    ),
}
engine_50 = gf.create_engine(segment_length=1.0, frequencies=[50.0])
ratios = {}
lines = [f"{'soil':40s} {'R_station':>10s} {'|Z_in|':>10s} {'ratio':>6s}"]
for label, soil in soils.items():
    r_st = engine_50.solve(station_alone(soil)).input_impedance()[0].real
    z_nw = abs(engine_50.solve(network(soil=soil)).input_impedance()[0])
    ratios[label] = z_nw / r_st
    lines.append(f"{label:40s} {r_st:6.2f} Ohm {z_nw:6.3f} Ohm {ratios[label]:6.1%}")
print("\n".join(lines))

    In every soil the network carries the fault current: its impedance is 2.3 to 14 % of the station alone. The two impedances see different soil. The station's electrodes, all within 2.5 m of the surface, see mainly the top layer; the network, some 240 m wide, sees mainly the bottom layer. The network impedance therefore follows \(\rho_2\) (0.29 Ω over 30 Ω·m, 0.46 Ω over 200 Ω·m, both with a 5 m top layer), and the reduction is largest for a resistive top over a conductive bottom and smallest the other way round. A thick resistive top layer (1000 Ω·m, 30 m) keeps the network at 2.4 Ω.

    2 Earth potential rise and touch voltages during an MV earth fault¶

    The earth potential rise (EPR) \(U_E = \lvert Z_\mathrm{in}\rvert\,I_E\) is the potential of the station earth against remote earth. A person who touches an accessible metal part bonded to an earth electrode and stands 1 m from it bridges the touch voltage \(U_T = \varphi_\mathrm{part} - \varphi_\mathrm{feet}\) (the prospective value, see T08). The touch points:

    • the station housing, 3 m × 2.5 m in the centre of the ring: feet 1 m from the middle of each wall, all round, none inside the housing;
    • the houses with a foundation earth electrode: metal parts on the outer walls (a service connection box, a tap, a gate), feet 1 m outside the foundation in 24 directions and on the arc round each corner (touch_voltage_envelope);
    • the old house: its service connection box, feet 1 m around it, none inside the house.

    They are evaluated on the mom solution, which is field-grade next to the foundations.

    In [10]:
    Copied! 
    field_engine = gf.create_engine(
    backend="mom", segment_length=1.0, frequencies=FREQUENCIES
)
field = field_engine.solve(world)
field_alone = field_engine.solve(alone)

# the station housing, 3 m x 2.5 m: its outline and the middle of each wall in m
HOUSING = [(-1.5, -1.25), (1.5, -1.25), (1.5, 1.25), (-1.5, 1.25)]
WALLS = [(1.5, 0.0), (0.0, 1.25), (-1.5, 0.0), (0.0, -1.25)]


def touch_station(res, wld, k=F50):
    # Largest |U_T| in V/A at the walls of the station housing.
    u = [
        gf.touch_voltage_at_part(
            res,
            wld,
            position=p,
            bonded_to=STATION,
            exclude=[HOUSING],
            frequency_index=k,
        )[1]
        for p in WALLS
    ]
    return np.abs(np.concatenate(u)).max()


def touch_houses(res, wld, k=F50):
    # Largest |U_T| in V/A 1 m outside each foundation, one value per house.
    largest = []
    for h in HOUSES:
        _, u = gf.touch_voltage_envelope(res, wld, electrode=h, frequency_index=k)
        largest.append(np.abs(u).max())
    return np.array(largest)


def touch_old_house(res, wld, k=F50):
    # Largest |U_T| in V/A around the service connection box of the old house.
    u = gf.touch_voltage_at_part(
        res,
        wld,
        position=OLD_BOX,
        bonded_to="old_house_box",
        exclude=[OLD_HOUSE],
        frequency_index=k,
    )[1]
    return np.abs(u).max()


# per ampere of I_E at 50 Hz: EPR, U_T at the station, the houses, the old house (V/A)
per_ampere = {
    "station alone": (
        abs(field_alone.electrode_potentials[STATION][F50]),
        touch_station(field_alone, alone),
        np.nan,
        np.nan,
    ),
    "with the network": (
        abs(field.electrode_potentials[STATION][F50]),
        touch_station(field, world),
        touch_houses(field, world).max(),
        touch_old_house(field, world),
    ),
}
WIDTHS = (7, 12, 11, 14)
print(
    f"{'per ampere, 50 Hz':18s} {'EPR':>7s} {'U_T station':>12s} {'U_T houses':>11s} {'U_T old house':>14s}"
)
for case, values in per_ampere.items():
    row = [
        f"{v:{w}.4f}" if np.isfinite(v) else f"{'-':>{w}s}"
        for v, w in zip(values, WIDTHS, strict=True)
    ]
    print(f"{case:18s} {' '.join(row)}  V/A")

    Two fault scenarios show what these per-ampere values mean. \(I_E\) is the part of the earth-fault current that flows into this earthing system; the share that the screens of the MV cables carry back (the reduction factor) is not computed by groundfield and is assumed to be taken off already. The permissible touch voltage \(U_{Tp}\) comes from the library's EN 50522 curve (gf.permissible_touch_voltage_en50522).

    Scenario MV neutral earthing \(I_E\) fault duration \(t_f\)
    A resonant (Petersen coil): residual current, the network keeps running 60 A not cleared
    B low-impedance, or a double earth fault: cleared by protection 1000 A 0.5 s

    The currents are examples, not data of a real network. The last column below is the largest \(I_E\) for which every touch voltage stays within \(U_{Tp}\).

    Without the network the station earth would rise to 9.8 V per ampere and expose a person at the housing to 3.6 V/A: in scenario A 216 V against the permissible 80 V. The station alone tolerates an uncleared fault current of only 22 A.

    With the network the EPR falls to 0.29 V/A, and both scenarios pass. The station housing, in the middle of its ring and of the network, sees only 0.065 V/A, the houses with a foundation earth electrode at most 0.15 V/A. The largest touch voltage is no longer at the station but at the old house without an earth electrode, 0.22 V/A. It sets the limits of the network: 362 A for a fault that is not cleared, 1018 A for one cleared in 0.5 s. In scenario B it reaches 221 V against 225 V, a margin of 2 %, smaller than the spread between the engines in section 5 (up to 3 % for touch voltages). In practice one would give that house an earth electrode of its own, or measure. Section 3 shows why it is the weak point.

    3 What potentials does the PEN transfer to the houses?¶

    The PEN connects every house to the station, so every house takes part in the potential rise. Its foundation is at the potential of its cluster, \(\varphi_\mathrm{house}\), which differs from the station's only by the voltage drop along the PEN. The protective conductor carries that potential into the house: it is a transferred potential. What a person outside the house bridges is the touch voltage, the difference to the ground 1 m outside the wall.

    The figure shows both for every house against its distance from the station, at 50 Hz and at 1 kHz.

    In [13]:
    Copied! 
    def centre(house):
    # Centre of a foundation: the mean of the vertices of its wires.
    wires = [e for e in world.electrodes if e.name in field.clusters[house]]
    return np.vstack([np.asarray(e.vertices)[:, :2] for e in wires]).mean(axis=0)


distance = np.array([np.hypot(*centre(h)) for h in HOUSES])
phi_station = field.electrode_potentials[STATION]
transfer, touch, old = {}, {}, {}
for k in (F50, F1K):
    phi_houses = np.array([field.electrode_potentials[h][k] for h in HOUSES])
    transfer[k] = np.abs(phi_houses / phi_station[k])
    touch[k] = touch_houses(field, world, k)
    old[k] = (
        abs(field.metadata["junction_potentials"]["old_house_box"][k]),
        touch_old_house(field, world, k),
    )

for k, label in ((F50, "50 Hz"), (F1K, "1 kHz")):
    print(
        f"{label}: house potentials {transfer[k].min():.1%} ... {transfer[k].max():.1%} of the station's; "
        f"U_T at the houses {touch[k].min():.3f} ... {touch[k].max():.3f} V/A, "
        f"largest {distance[np.argmax(touch[k])]:.0f} m from the station"
    )
    print(
        f"       old house: potential {old[k][0]:.3f} V/A, U_T {old[k][1]:.3f} V/A ({old[k][1] / old[k][0]:.0%} of it)"
    )
pe_b = SCENARIOS["B"][0] * abs(phi_station[F50]) * transfer[F50]
print(
    f"scenario B: protective conductors of the houses at {pe_b.min():.0f} ... {pe_b.max():.0f} V against remote earth"
)

    At 50 Hz every house carries 97 to 100 % of the station's potential: the voltage drop along the PEN is small against the EPR. In scenario B the protective conductor of every house rises to 280 to 287 V against remote earth for the 0.5 s of the fault. The touch voltage at a house with a foundation earth electrode is only about half of that potential, 0.13 to 0.15 V/A, because its own electrode and its neighbours lift the ground around it. It grows towards the edge of the network, where fewer neighbours lift the ground; the largest is at a corner house, 116 m from the station.

    The old house at the end of the eastern cable has the potential of the cabinet, 0.28 V/A, and 79 % of it appears as touch voltage: nothing lifts the ground under it but the far field of the network. That is the classic hazard of a transferred potential, and the foundation earth electrodes of the other houses are what keeps it small there.

    At 1 kHz the picture changes: the potentials fall along the PEN, to 62 % at the far ends. What counts is the cable length from the station, not the distance; the western main joins its first house 13.5 m from the station ring, the eastern one after 3.5 m, hence the two branches near the station. The houses close to the station now carry the higher 1 kHz EPR and have the largest touch voltages, up to 0.20 V/A.

    The surface potential at 50 Hz (per ampere of \(I_E\)) shows the whole village lifted with the station: every foundation sits in its own potential funnel on a common plateau.

    4 What changes at 1 kHz?¶

    Below 1 kHz the soil stays quasi-static: an earth electrode is a resistance. What changes with frequency is the PEN: its series impedance \(R + j\omega L\) grows with the angular frequency \(\omega\), and the remote houses contribute less (T04). This matters for the harmonics of a residual earth-fault current, for earth testers that measure at a frequency other than 50 Hz, and for the frequency-dependent model of the network that a network calculation needs.

    From 50 Hz to 1 kHz the network impedance rises by 36 % to 0.40 Ω, at a phase angle of 31°; the station alone stays at 9.9 Ω. The station's own electrodes take a larger share of the current (2.7 % instead of 1.75 %), and more houses help less: going from 30 to 80 houses lowers \(\lvert Z_\mathrm{in}\rvert\) to 0.47 of its value at 50 Hz but only to 0.62 at 1 kHz.

    For a planner this means: an impedance measured or computed at 50 Hz is not the impedance for the harmonics of a residual current; the touch voltage per ampere of a 1 kHz current is up to 0.20 V/A here, a third more than at 50 Hz. The rho-f model of T04 carries \(Z(f)\) into a network calculation. The earth-return model matters at these frequencies: the default sommerfeld is the reference, while carson_series reads the reactance of LV networks with short service drops too high (earth return).

    5 How far can the numbers be trusted?¶

    Three free checks have already passed: Kirchhoff's current law (the leakage currents add up to \(I_E\)), the fall of \(Z_\mathrm{in}\) with every added house, and diagnose without findings. Four more follow: the discretisation, a second current model, a second Green's function, and a method that shares no kernel with the others. The section ends with the engines' known limits that apply here.

    Discretisation¶

    The segment length is halved twice:

    Current model and Green's function¶

    image and mom share the image kernels but not the current model. mom and mom_sommerfeld share the discretisation but not the Green's function: the Tagg/Sunde image series against the Sommerfeld integral evaluated by quadrature. The first pair runs on the full network; mom_sommerfeld is slower, so it runs on a small variant with five houses.

)

    The two current models differ by 1.2 % at 50 Hz and 0.7 % at 1 kHz; the fem check below shows that most of it is the point kernel of mom, which reads 1 to 2 % low. At the houses the image touch voltages lie about 3 % above the mom values, and every call warns that they are impedance-grade: near meshes and bonded clusters mom is the field-grade engine. The two Green's functions agree to about 1e-8: the image series is right for this soil.

    What fem can and cannot do here¶

    fem solves the volume problem by finite elements and shares no kernel with the integral engines (fem). Its axisymmetric model takes rods on one axis and rings around it, to about 1e-4, in a fraction of a second. The station's ring alone is such a world:

    In [22]:
    Copied! 
    def ring_alone():
    ring = gf.create_world(soil=SOIL.to_soil(np.random.default_rng(0)))
    gf.create_electrode(
        ring, "ring", name="ring", center=(0.0, 0.0, 0.6), radius=4.0, wire_radius=0.005
    )
    gf.create_source(ring, attached_to="ring", magnitude=1.0)
    return ring


with warnings.catch_warnings():
    warnings.simplefilter("ignore", gf.ExperimentalBackendWarning)
    ring_fem = gf.create_engine(backend="fem", segment_length=0.5).solve(ring_alone())

print(
    f"station ring alone: fem   {r_fem:.4f} Ohm (error estimate {ring_fem.metadata['fem_error_estimate']:.1e})"
)

    On the ring image lies within 0.1 % of fem (whose error estimate is 1.4e-3), mom 1.2 % below it, the pattern of the validation page. The station with its four rods off the axis needs the three-dimensional model; for a station earth of similar size (the AP1 station of the validation, a 4 m × 4 m ring with three 4 m rods) the fem page reports 75 to 140 s and about 4.3 GB, more than this example may spend. The network is refused before any mesh is built: 187 ports against a limit of 100, with a predicted solve time of 920 minutes (without the optional fem3d extra the call stops earlier, with an ImportError that names the extra). fem is a reference for single earthing systems, not a network engine.

    Known limits of the engines that apply here¶

    From the known limitations, the ones that bear on this example:

    • Uniform current per wire (image): impedances of meshes like these foundations are 0.4 to 0.7 % above one current per segment; touch and step voltages next to them are only impedance-grade, hence mom for the field values here.
    • Point kernel (mom): grounding resistances 0.9 to 1.9 % low, as measured above.
    • Earth return: carson_series reads the reactance of generated LV networks 4 to 21 % high at 1 kHz against sommerfeld; use the default.
    • Generated networks: the service drops of the outer rows pass 0.2 m above the side wires of the centre-row houses without inductive coupling to them (moved aside, at most 0.006 % with an insulated PEN); the 1 kHz reactance depends on where cables and drops meet the foundations; and the star topology with one cabinet per building group is a modelling choice: for the default 30-house network it reads a reactance at 1 kHz 55 to 64 % above that of the former cabinet strip with its parallel drops.
    • Quasi-static soil: valid below 1 kHz; impulse and lightning currents are out of scope.

    Summary¶

    • Global earthing. The 30-house network lowers the impedance at the station from 9.9 Ω (the station alone) to 0.29 Ω at 50 Hz, 2.9 %; 98 % of the fault current leaves the soil at the houses. In five soils of the AP1 grid the ratio is 2.3 to 14 %; the network impedance follows the bottom layer.
    • Earth fault. With the network the EPR is 0.29 V/A; the touch voltages are 0.065 V/A at the station housing and at most 0.15 V/A at the houses with a foundation earth electrode. Scenario A (60 A, not cleared): at most 13 V against 80 V, where the station alone would give 216 V. Scenario B (1 kA, 0.5 s): 221 V against 225 V, at the old house.
    • Transferred potentials. At 50 Hz every house carries 97 to 100 % of the station's potential. A foundation earth electrode keeps the touch voltage at about half of it; at a house without one it is 79 %.
    • 1 kHz. \(\lvert Z_\mathrm{in}\rvert\) rises by 36 %, the far houses fall to 62 % of the station's potential, more houses help less, and the touch voltage per ampere near the station rises by a third.
    • Trust. 1 m segments are converged to 3e-5; image and mom agree within 1.2 % on the impedance and 3.4 % on the touch voltages; two Green's functions agree to 1e-8; fem confirms the station ring to 0.1 % and refuses the network.

    Limits of this example¶

    • One generated network. The generator's defaults in one soil, one realisation: not a real network. A study runs the parameter space (house counts, penetration of foundation earth electrodes, soils) with sweeps or Monte Carlo (how-to guide Sweeps and Monte Carlo).
    • Bare foundations. The concrete encasement of real foundation earth electrodes changes their resistance (case study E02 and the concrete shells page).
    • The MV side is not modelled. No MV cable screens, no neighbouring stations connected through them, no reduction factor: \(I_E\) is an input. In a real network the cable screens connect further station earths and lower the impedance further.
    • Only this LV network. Water pipes, other utilities, neighbouring LV networks and the houses' own installations are not part of the model.
    • Touch voltages are prospective proxies. Feet 1 m from the station walls and the house foundations stand for the real touch points; no body, shoe or surface-layer resistance is included. Step voltages are not assessed (T08 shows how), nor are the stress voltages on the LV installations.
    • EN 50522 enters only through the library's permissible touch voltage curve; the scenario currents are examples.
